Discovering ancient cities 
Satellite imaging is helping to locate ruins of long-lost cities. 
Can satellite paint the past archaeological face? 
The long-lost city of Altinum, near the modern-day coast of what is now Italy, was one of the 
richest cities in the Roman Empire, a meeting place for traders from around the ancient world. In 
the turbulent politics of the 5th century, however, as the Empire was falling apart, Altinum’s 
residents fled, fearing they would be overrun by invading forces. They left a ghost town behind, 
full of decaying villas. After much of the stone was used to build a new town nearby — known as 
Venice — Altinum was buried below fertile agricultural land. Historians knew the city had 
existed but its remains were hidden from view. 
Now, more than 1500 years on, Altinum has appeared again. Using sophisticated aerial 
photography, a research team of earth scientists and archaeologists at the University of Padova 
have created a picture of how Altinum looked when it was abandoned — a unique time capsule of 
a city in the final years of the Roman Empire. But what do you take pictures of when ruins are 
buried? 
Research has shown that the moisture content of plants at archaeological sites varies according to 
the presence of man-made structures under the topsoil. However, the Padova team also suspected 
that infrared photography* would reveal which crops were growing directly above the ruins at 
Altinum and which were growing elsewhere here, and that infrared photographs could therefore 
provide a clear view of the once-great city. 
This suspicion led them to commission a plane with sensors to take photographs of the fields 
during a particularly dry period. The resulting image highlighted patches where the plants could 
only draw upon a thin layer of soil, owing to the stonework beneath. Lighter markings pointed to 
private houses or other public constructions, while dark patches indicated where canals had been. 
‘The images were stunning,’ says Professor Paolo Mozzi. ‘I immediately understood that this was 
a big step beyond what was known.’ The professor explains that for him and his colleagues it was 
once impossible to imagine the complexity of the city, ‘but we can now begin to reconstruct 
exactly what Altinum must have looked like, and all without any actual digging.’ 
Taking to the skies to get a better view of the past is hardly a fresh breakthrough. It started by 
chance a century ago when men engaged in military map-making realised that the land they were 
flying over was dotted with traces of vanished settlements. Only in the past few years, however, 
have archaeologists realised the potential of digital sensors that can record data across the 
electromagnetic spectrum.

3 
 
 
In Cambodia, archaeologists from the University of Sydney have used satellite technology to 
prove that Angkor was the largest city in the pre-industrial world, comparable in size to 
present-day Los Angeles in the US. Ground-penetrating radar images have highlighted a vast 
network of ancient canals stretching out well beyond the famous temple, as far as the suburbs 
where up to one million people lived between the 9th and 13th centuries. In the same way, on 
Easter Island in the Pacific Ocean, scientists from the University of Hawaii have exposed the 
paths which the early Polynesian people used to drag the huge moai, the island’s unusual stone 
statues, into position. 
The prospect of such groundbreaking discoveries led the National Aeronautics and Space 
Administration (NASA) in the US to create a ‘space archaeology’ division under its Research 
Opportunities in Space and Earth Science Program. Dr Bill Saturno from the University of Boston 
is working closely with NASA to unearth the secrets of the Mayan Empire, a once powerful 
civilisation that ruled in Central America for 2000 years before it mysteriously collapsed. Using 
NASA’s commercial satellite photography, Saturno hit the headlines when he uncovered a series 
of large Mayan sites under the dense rainforest of Guatemala. 
‘We used a satellite called IKONOS,’ explains Saturno. ‘It records data in four bands of light.’ In 
the near-infrared images, rainforest shows up red and low-lying wet ground appears blue, but an 
uncharted region around San Bartolo showed some patches of unexpected yellow colouration. 
This Saturno spotted a correlation between these and the location of known archaeological sites. 
The effect is caused by the decaying remains of the limestone which the Mayans used for 
building. At near-infrared wavelengths, this discolouration becomes visible. 
When Saturno left the lab and ventured deep into unmapped rainforest to see if the satellite 
predictions lined up with on-the-ground reality, he was not disappointed. He found all kinds of 
reconstructions from modest stone platforms which would have supported family dwellings to 
vast palaces where wall paintings of traditional legends are still visible. ‘We’re used to seeing 
satellite images of modern cities, but being able to see the outlines of houses built 1400 years ago 
is truly remarkable,’ he says. He is not the only archaeologist to think so. 
Dr Sarah Parcak has revealed over 100 previously unknown sites in Egypt’s Nile Delta region, 
including temples and tombs, which were built on sandy mounds to protect them from the rising 
water of the Nile. The river hasn’t flooded for years, but ever-growing modern towns have 
covered up the traces of the past. But, as Parcak explains: ‘With satellite imagery I’m able to 
identify shapes and patterns that indicate the presence of sites, even if they’re buried.’ She seems 
bemused by the attitude of others in the field: ‘I can’t believe that so few other Egyptologists are 
doing this kind of work,’ she says. ‘There are still so many sites to be found!’
